gr-sva.title: Subject–Verb Agreement
gr-sva.html:
Singular / Plural  ·  + 12 rules

The verb must match its subject in number. Find the real subject first. Words in between do not count.

PAGE 1
The Basic MatchFind the real subject, then match the verb

Start here: Which verb? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Subject first, verb second. Never match the verb to the nearest noun by habit.

1.1 Singular or plural?

SINGULAR SUBJECTtakes is / was / has / V+s The teacher is kind.
PLURAL SUBJECTtakes are / were / have / V The teachers are kind.
A AND Btwo persons = plural Tea and coffee are ready.
ONE IDEA WITH ANDone thing = singular Bread and butter is my breakfast.
OR / NORverb agrees with the subject NEAREST to it Either you or he is wrong. ALONG WITH, AS WELL AS, WITH ignore it; verb agrees with the first subject The captain, along with the team, is here.
M E M O R Y H A C K | C R O S S O U T T H E E X T R A S

Cross out everything between the subject and the verb. The bouquet (of red roses) is lovely. Cross out "of red roses" and the verb is obvious.

PAGE 2
Tricky SubjectsWords that look plural but are not, and the reverse

2.1 Special nouns and phrases (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

These three groups are the most common exam traps.

2.2 More rules to remember

A NUMBER OF / THE NUMBER OFa number of = plural, the number of = singular A number of students are absent. The number of students is small.
ONE OF THE + PLURAL NOUNverb is singular One of my friends is a doctor.
EACH / EVERYalways singular Every boy and girl has a book.
COLLECTIVE NOUNSone unit = singular; members acting separately = plural The jury has given its verdict. The jury are divided.
MANY Asingular Many a man has failed.
THERE IS / AREverb matches the noun AFTER it There are five boys. There is a pen.
WHO / THAT / WHICHverb matches the noun before it He is one of the boys who are late.
PAIR WORDSscissors, trousers, spectacles: plural, but "a pair of" is singular A pair of shoes is here.
UNCOUNTABLE NOUNSfurniture, advice, luggage, information: singular The furniture is new.
E X A M T R A P S W I T H

In one of the ... who sentences the verb is plural: He is one of the students who have passed. But the only one who is singular: He is the only one who has passed.

M E M O R Y H A C K | N E W S = N O P L U R A L

News, mathematics, physics, economics, politics, measles: they end in -s but are singular. No news is good news.

PAGE 3

Traps, Practice and Recap

The mistakes examiners love, then test yourself

3.1 Quick decision for or / nor and compound subjects (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

And adds. Or picks. With ignores.

3.2 Favourite exam traps
WRONG
RIGHT
WHY
The list of items are on the desk
The list is on the deskhead noun is list
Mathematics are difficult
Mathematics is difficultsingular subject
Each of the boys are present
Each of the boys is presenteach = singular
A number of students is absent
A number of students are absenta number of = plural
Neither he nor I is going
Neither he nor I am goingnearest subject is I
The police is here
The police are herepolice is plural
There is two pens on the desk
There are two pensverb matches the noun after
The furniture are new
The furniture is newuncountable noun

3.3 Mixed practice: choose the right verb

1. The quality of the mangoes (is / are) poor.

2. Each of the girls (has / have) a prize.

3. Neither the teacher nor the students (was / were) present.

4. Economics (is / are) an interesting subject.

5. A number of books (is / are) missing.

6. The number of books (is / are) small.

7. Bread and butter (is / are) my usual breakfast.

8. One of the boys (is / are) absent.

9. The poor (needs / need) our help.

10. There (is / are) many reasons for this.

Answers: 1 is, 2 has, 3 were, 4 is, 5 are, 6 is, 7 is, 8 is, 9 need, 10 are.

6 0 - S E C O N D R E C A P

Find the real subject, ignore of / with / along with.

And = plural, or / nor = nearest noun.

Each, every, either, neither, one of = singular.

News, maths, economics = singular; police, people, cattle = plural.

A number of = plural, the number of = singular.

There is / are follows the noun after it.

gr-tenses.title: Tenses
gr-tenses.html:
12 tenses  ·  + time words + traps

A tense tells you when something happens (past, present, future) and how (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous). In CUET, time words and a handful of classic traps decide almost every question.

PAGE 1
The 12 TensesForms, meanings and the time words that signal them

Start here: the Tense Finder (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Underline the time word first. It names the tense before you even read the verb.

1.1 The twelve tenses at a glance

PRESENT SIMPLEV1 (+s/es) She writes daily.
PRESENT CONTINUOUSis/am/are + V-ing She is writing now.
PRESENT PERFECThas/have + V3 She has written it. PRESENT PERFECT CONT. has/have been + V-ing She has been writing for an hour.
PAST SIMPLE
V2She wrote yesterday.
PAST CONTINUOUSwas/were + V-ing She was writing when I called.
PAST PERFECThad + V3 She had written before I came. PAST PERFECT CONT. had been + V-ing She had been writing for an hour.
FUTURE SIMPLEwill + V1 She will write tomorrow.
FUTURE CONTINUOUSwill be + V-ing She will be writing at 5.
FUTURE PERFECTwill have + V3 She will have written by 5. FUTURE PERFECT CONT. will have been + V-ing She will have been writing for an hour by 5.

1.2 Time words tell you the tense

SIMPLE PRESENTalways, usually, often, never, every day, on Sundays
PRESENT PERFECTalready, yet, just, ever, never, so far, recently, lately
PRESENT CONTINUOUSnow, at the moment, today, currently, look!, listen!
PAST SIMPLEyesterday, last week, ago, in 2010, once, then
PAST CONTINUOUSwhile, when (during an action), at that time, all day
PAST PERFECTbefore, after, by the time, already (in the past), had...when
M E M O R Y H A C K | S I N C E & F O R

Since = point, For = period. Since 2020, since Monday, since I was ten. / For six years, for two hours, for a long time. Both take the perfect tense: I have lived here since 2020 / for six years.

PAGE 2
Rules That Win Marks
The patterns CUET tests again and again

2.1 Which tense after if, when, before, until? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Three questions catch most tense errors in the exam.

2.2 Present perfect, past simple and special patterns

PRESENT PERFECTresult matters now or time is unfinished I have finished my work. She has lived here for years.
PAST SIMPLEfinished, named time I finished it yesterday. We met in 2019.
UNIVERSAL TRUTHalways present simple Water boils at 100°C.
HARDLY / NO SOONERpast perfect first Hardly had he left when it rained. No sooner had she come than...
WISH / AS IF / IT IS TIMEfollowed by the past It is time we left. I wish I knew. He talks as if he were king.
SINCE CLAUSEpast in since-clause, perfect in main It has been five years since we met.
USED TO + V1past habit, not now I used to walk daily.
SEQUENCE OF TENSESpast main verb → past second verb He said that he was ill.
TIMETABLESpresent simple for the future The train leaves at six.
E X A M T R A P S W I T H

Never use the present perfect with a finished-time word: I have seen him yesterday → I saw him yesterday.

No will after if / when: if it will rain → if it rains.

No -ing for stative verbs: I am knowing → I know.

M E M O R Y H A C K | P - E - R - F - E - C - T

Perfect tense = have/had/will have + V3. Ask: "Is the action complete, with a link to another time?" If yes, perfect. If it is just a finished event with a named time, use the simple past.

PAGE 3

Traps, Practice and Recap

The mistakes examiners love, then test yourself

3.1 Past simple or present perfect? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

A finished time word and the present perfect never go together.

3.2 Favourite exam traps
WRONG
RIGHT
WHY
I have seen him yesterday
I saw him yesterdayfinished time word If it will rain, we will stay If it rains, we will stay present after if
I am knowing the answer
I know the answerstative verb When we reached, the film started the film had started earlier action = had + V3 Hardly he had left when... Hardly had he left when... hardly + had + subject
I live here since six years
I have lived here for six yearsfor + period
She has gone to Paris in 2019
She went to Paris in 2019named year = past I wish I knew it (past regret)
I wish I had known itpast regret = had + V3

3.3 Mixed practice: choose the right tense

1. I (have lived / lived) here since 2015.

2. She (went / has gone) to Paris last year.

3. When we reached, the film (started / had started).

4. I will call you when he (will arrive / arrives).

5. He (is knowing / knows) the answer.

6. Hardly (had / has) he left when it rained.

7. If you (will study / study) hard, you will pass.

8. The sun (rises / rose) in the east.

9. I (am waiting / have been waiting) for two hours.

10. She (has finished / finished) the report yesterday.

Answers: 1 have lived, 2 went, 3 had started, 4 arrives, 5 knows, 6 had, 7 study, 8 rises, 9 have been waiting, 10 finished.

6 0 - S E C O N D R E C A P

Time word first: yesterday/ago → past simple; since/for/already/yet → present perfect; now → continuous.

Since = point, for = period.

Earlier of two past actions → had + V3.

After if / when / before → present for the future.

know, like, want never take -ing.

Hardly / no sooner → had + subject + V3.

gr-articles.title: Articles
gr-articles.html:
A / An / The  ·  + zero article

Articles are the tiny words a, an, the. They look easy but they decide many CUET marks. Think about sound, first mention and specific or general.

PAGE 1

A, An and The

Which article goes before which noun

Start here: Which article? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Ask: "Which one?" If the listener knows, use the.

1.1 A or an? Listen to the sound, not the spelling

AN + VOWEL SOUNDa, e, i, o, u sound an apple, an hour, an honest man
A + CONSONANT SOUNDeven if spelled with a vowel a university, a European, a one-rupee note
AN + SILENT Hhour, honest, honour, heir an heir, an honour

1.2 When to use THE

ALREADY MENTIONEDsecond mention I met a boy. The boy was kind.
UNIQUE THINGSonly one exists the sun, the moon, the sky
SUPERLATIVESthe best, the first She is the tallest girl. RIVERS, SEAS, OCEANS also mountain ranges the Ganga, the Himalayas NEWSPAPERS, HOLY BOOKS special names the Hindu, the Gita
THE + ADJECTIVEa whole group the rich, the poor
M E M O R Y H A C K | S O U N D N O T S P E L L I N G

Say the word aloud. an hour (silent h, vowel sound) but a university (starts with a "yoo" sound). The first sound decides a or an.

PAGE 2
Rules and OmissionWhen to skip the article and special patterns

2.1 Do I need an article here? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Place names used for their purpose take no article.

2.2 Rules that win marks

PROPER NOUNSno article India is large. Delhi is a city. LANGUAGES, SUBJECTS no article She speaks French. I like Science.
MEALSno article, unless specific We had lunch. We had a good lunch.
SUCH A / WHAT A / QUITE Aa goes after such, what, quite Such a nice day! What a pity! HALF, DOUBLE, ALL, BOTH article comes AFTER these Half the cake, both the boys MANY A, A FEW, A LITTLE meaning of few: a few = some, few = hardly any I have a few friends.
E X A M T R A P S W I T H

Never put an article before plural nouns used in general: The dogs are loyal (about all dogs) → Dogs are loyal.

Never use a before uncountable nouns: an advice → a piece of advice.

M E M O R Y H A C K | N A M E S N E E D N O N A M E - T A G

Names of people, countries, cities, languages and subjects wear no article (India, Hindi, Maths). Rivers, seas, ranges wear the (the Ganga, the Alps).

PAGE 3

Traps, Practice and Recap

The mistakes examiners love, then test yourself

3.1 Last check: Which article now? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Sound first, then definite or general.

3.2 Favourite exam traps
WRONG
RIGHT
WHY
She is an university student
She is a university studentyoo sound = consonant
I waited for a hour
I waited for an hoursilent h
The Hindi is easy
Hindi is easyno article before language
He gave me an advice
He gave me some adviceadvice is uncountable
A Ganga is holy
The Ganga is holyrivers take the
She is tallest girl in class
She is the tallest girlsuperlative needs the What nice a day! What a nice day! what + a + adjective
He goes to the school daily
He goes to school dailyplace for its purpose

3.3 Mixed practice: fill in a / an / the / no article

1. He is ___ honest man.

2. She plays ___ guitar well.

3. I saw ___ owl. ___ owl was huge.

4. ___ Himalayas are in the north.

5. He is ___ one-eyed man.

6. She goes to ___ church every Sunday.

7. ___ sun rises in the east.

8. It was ___ unusual event.

9. Ravi is ___ best player in the team.

10. ___ gold is a precious metal.

Answers: 1 an, 2 the (musical instrument), 3 an / The, 4 The, 5 a, 6 (no article), 7 The, 8 an, 9 the, 10 (no article).

6 0 - S E C O N D R E C A P

Sound decides a / an: an hour, a university.

The = known, unique, superlative, rivers, ranges.

No article: names, languages, subjects, meals, general plurals.

Musical instruments take the: play the guitar.

Such a / what a: article after such / what.

Half / both / all + the.

gr-prepositions.title: Prepositions
gr-prepositions.html:
In / On / At  ·  + fixed pairs

A preposition links a noun to the rest of the sentence. CUET tests time and place, fixed word pairs and which preposition follows which word.

PAGE 1
Time and PlaceIn, on, at and their cousins

Start here: In, on or at? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

In is big, on is a surface, at is a point.

1.1 The three big ones

IN (TIME)

months, years, seasons, parts of day

in June, in 2020, in the morning

ON (TIME)

days and dates

on Sunday, on 5 May

AT (TIME)

clock time, festivals, night

at 6 pm, at night, at Diwali

IN (PLACE)

inside a space or town

in a room, in Delhi

ON (PLACE)

touching a surface

on the table, on the wall

AT (PLACE)

a point or a building as a place

at the gate, at the station

1.2 Other must-know prepositions

SINCE / FORsince = point, for = period since 2019, for two years
BY / UNTILby = deadline, until = continues till Finish by 5. Wait until 5.
BETWEEN / AMONGbetween two, among many between you and me, among friends
BESIDE / BESIDESbeside = next to, besides = in addition Besides Hindi, she knows French.
DURING / WHILEduring + noun, while + clause during the war, while he slept
IN / WITHINwithin = inside a limit Return within a week.
M E M O R Y H A C K | I N - O N - A T F U N N E L

Time goes from big to small: in (year, month) → on (day, date) → at (clock time). In 2024, on 5 May, at 6 pm.

PAGE 2
Fixed PairsWords that always come with one preposition

2.1 Which preposition after this word? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Most prepositions here are fixed. Learn them as pairs.

2.2 Pairs you must know

ADJECTIVE + OFafraid, proud, jealous, fond, aware, capable, short proud of you, fond of music
ADJECTIVE + TOknown, kind, married, similar, superior, junior married to, superior to, prefer A to B
ADJECTIVE + IN / AT / WITHinterested in, good at, weak in, angry with, satisfied with good at maths, interested in art
VERB + ONdepend, rely, insist, focus, congratulate on rely on him, congratulate her on her win
VERB + FORwait, ask, search, apologise, look for wait for him, search for a pen
VERB + FROM / WITHsuffer from, differ from, agree with, deal with suffer from fever, deal with it
E X A M T R A P S W I T H

Prefer takes to, never than: I prefer tea than coffee → I prefer tea to coffee.

Discuss takes no preposition: discuss about it → discuss it.

Reach takes none: reach to Delhi → reach Delhi.

M E M O R Y H A C K | N O P R E P O S I T I O N G A N G

Verbs that take no preposition: discuss, reach, enter, attend, resemble, order, request. She resembles her mother. He entered the room.

PAGE 3

Traps, Practice and Recap

The mistakes examiners love, then test yourself

3.1 Decide quickly: preposition or none? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Two short checks catch most wrong prepositions.

3.2 Favourite exam traps
WRONG
RIGHT
WHY
I prefer tea than coffee
I prefer tea to coffeeprefer + to
We discussed about the plan
We discussed the plandiscuss takes no preposition
He is good in maths
He is good at mathsgood at
She is married with him
She is married to himmarried to
I was born at 2004
I was born in 2004in + year
The book is in the table
The book is on the tableon + surface
He is senior than me
He is senior to mesenior to
She is afraid from dogs
She is afraid of dogsafraid of

3.3 Mixed practice: fill in the preposition

1. The meeting is ___ Monday.

2. He was born ___ 1999.

3. She is fond ___ music.

4. I am interested ___ painting.

5. They are waiting ___ the bus.

6. He is junior ___ me.

7. Please divide the sweets ___ the two boys.

8. The sweets are shared ___ the three of us.

9. She is angry ___ her brother.

10. He apologised ___ being late.

Answers: 1 on, 2 in, 3 of, 4 in, 5 for, 6 to, 7 between, 8 among, 9 with, 10 for.

6 0 - S E C O N D R E C A P

In = month, year; on = day, date; at = clock time, point.

Since = point, for = period.

Between two, among many.

Prefer, senior, junior + to.

Discuss, reach, enter, attend need no preposition.

Learn the pairs: good at, afraid of, depend on.

gr-pronouns.title: Pronouns
gr-pronouns.html:
Case & Agreement  ·  + who / whom

A pronoun takes the place of a noun. CUET asks about case (I or me), agreement with the noun, and who / whom, each other.

PAGE 1
Types and CaseSubject, object and possessive forms

Start here: I or me? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Doer = subject form, receiver = object form.

1.1 Pronoun forms

I

me, my, mine

I like it.

YOUyou, your, yours You are kind.
HE / SHEhim / her He met her.
WEus, our, ours We saw them.
THEYthem, their, theirs They helped us.
ITit, its Its tail is long.
WHOwhom, whose Whom did you meet?
REFLEXIVEmyself, himself, themselves She hurt herself.

1.2 Joined pronouns and "between"

BETWEEN / EXCEPT / BUT + PRONOUNalways object form Between you and me. Nobody but him came. THAN / AS (COMPARISON) finish the sentence in your head She is taller than I (am).
ORDER OF PRONOUNSIn good: 2nd, 3rd, 1st; in bad: 1st first You, he and I won. I and he were wrong.
M E M O R Y H A C K | D R O P T H E O T H E R P E R S O N

Cross out the extra name. Ravi and (I / me) went. → "I went", so Ravi and I went. She gave it to Ravi and (I / me). → "to me", so Ravi and me.

PAGE 2
Agreement and Special PronounsMatching the noun, plus who, whom, each other

2.1 Which pronoun fits? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

The pronoun must match its noun in person and number.

2.2 Rules that win marks

WHO / WHOMwho = subject, whom = object Who called? Whom did you call?
EACH OTHER / ONE ANOTHEReach other = two, one another = more Ram and Sita love each other.
REFLEXIVEonly when the subject acts on itself He hurt himself. Not: Myself went EITHER, NEITHER, EACH, EVERYONE singular, so use his / her Everyone must bring his or her book.
POSSESSIVE NO APOSTROPHEits, yours, hers, ours, theirs The dog wagged its tail.
RELATIVE PRONOUNSwho = person, which = thing, that = both The man who came is my uncle.
E X A M T R A P S W I T H

Its (belongs to it) has no apostrophe; it's means "it is": The dog wagged it's tail → its.

Whom follows a preposition: To who → To whom.

M E M O R Y H A C K | W H O O R W H O M

Try he / him. If "he" fits, use who; if "him" fits, use whom. (Who / Whom) did you meet? → "You met him" → whom.

PAGE 3

Traps, Practice and Recap

The mistakes examiners love, then test yourself

3.1 Who, whom or whose? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Substitute he or him to decide.

3.2 Favourite exam traps
WRONG
RIGHT
WHY
Between you and I
Between you and mebetween + object
She is taller than me
She is taller than Ithan I (am) The dog wagged it's tail
The dog wagged its tailpossessive: no apostrophe Who did you meet? Whom did you meet? object of "meet" Everyone must bring their pen (exam style)
Everyone must bring his or her peneveryone is singular
He and me went
He and I wentsubject form
Myself was late
I was lateno reflexive as subject
The two friends hate one another
The two friends hate each othertwo = each other

3.3 Mixed practice: choose the right pronoun

1. Between you and (I / me), this is a secret.

2. (Who / Whom) did you invite?

3. She is as tall as (I / me).

4. The dog wagged (its / it's) tail.

5. He hurt (him / himself) while cooking.

6. Ram and (I / me) are friends.

7. The man (who / which) called is my uncle.

8. Each boy must bring (his / their) own pen.

9. This book is (my / mine).

10. Ravi and Sita like (each other / one another).

Answers: 1 me, 2 Whom, 3 I, 4 its, 5 himself, 6 I, 7 who, 8 his, 9 mine, 10 each other.

6 0 - S E C O N D R E C A P

Subject form before the verb, object form after verb / preposition.

Between, except, but + object.

Than / as: finish the sentence in your head.

Who = he, whom = him.

Its has no apostrophe.

Each, either, neither, everyone = singular.

Each other = two, one another = more.

gr-adj-adv.title: Adjectives & Adverbs
gr-adj-adv.html:
Describe & modify  ·  + degrees

An adjective describes a noun; an adverb describes a verb, an adjective or another adverb. CUET tests which to choose, degrees of comparison, and word order.

PAGE 1

Adjective or Adverb?

Which word to use and how to tell

Start here: Adjective or adverb? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Adjectives describe things, adverbs describe actions.

1.1 Common patterns

ADJECTIVE + -LYmakes an adverb quick → quickly, careful → carefully
SAME FORM BOTH WAYSfast, hard, late, early, daily He runs fast. A fast train.
DIFFERENT MEANINGhard / hardly, late / lately, near / nearly He works hard. He hardly works.
LINKING VERBSbe, seem, look, feel, taste, sound take adjectives She looks pale.
GOOD / WELLgood = adjective, well = adverb She sings well. It is a good song.
ENOUGHafter adjective / adverb, before noun tall enough, enough time
M E M O R Y H A C K | H A R D V S H A R D L Y

hard = with effort, hardly = almost not. He works hard. / He hardly works. Likewise late = not on time, lately = recently.

PAGE 2
Degrees and OrderPositive, comparative, superlative and word order

2.1 Which degree? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Two = -er and than. Three or more = the -est.

2.2 Rules that win marks

SHORT WORDS-er / -est tall, taller, tallest
LONG WORDSmore / most beautiful, more beautiful, most beautiful
IRREGULARgood-better-best, bad-worse-worst, many-more-most better, worse
LATIN COMPARATIVESsenior, junior, superior, inferior take TO not than He is senior to me.
ELDER / OLDERelder = family only my elder brother; older than me
FARTHER / FURTHERfarther = distance, further = more farther away, further details
ORDER OF ADJECTIVESopinion, size, age, colour, origin, material a lovely small old red Indian wooden box
DOUBLE COMPARISONnever more + -er more taller → taller
ABSOLUTE ADJECTIVESunique, perfect, complete: no degrees more perfect
E X A M T R A P S W I T H

Comparative + than, superlative + the: She is more smarter than me → She is smarter than me.

He is the more tall → He is taller.

Fewer for countable, less for uncountable: fewer pens, less water.

M E M O R Y H A C K | O S A S C O M P

Adjective order: Opinion, Size, Age, Shape, Colour, Origin, Material, Purpose. a beautiful old Chinese silk dress.

PAGE 3

Traps, Practice and Recap

The mistakes examiners love, then test yourself

3.1 Few, a few, little, a little? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

a few / a little = some. few / little = hardly any.

3.2 Favourite exam traps
WRONG
RIGHT
WHY
She sings good
She sings welladverb for a verb
He is more taller than me
He is taller than meno double comparison
He is senior than me
He is senior to mesenior takes to
The soup tastes badly
The soup tastes badlinking verb + adjective
He works hardly
He works hardhardly = almost not
This is the most unique gift
This is a unique giftno degrees for unique
Less students came
Fewer students camecountable = fewer
She is the elder of the three
She is the eldest of the threethree = superlative

3.3 Mixed practice: choose the correct word

1. She dances (beautiful / beautifully).

2. The flowers smell (sweet / sweetly).

3. He is (more clever / cleverer) than his brother.

4. This is the (best / better) film of the year.

5. She is junior (than / to) me.

6. He (hard / hardly) ever visits us.

7. There is (few / little) milk left.

8. (Fewer / Less) people attended.

9. Ravi is the (taller / tallest) of the three.

10. She speaks (good / well).

Answers: 1 beautifully, 2 sweet, 3 cleverer, 4 best, 5 to, 6 hardly, 7 little, 8 Fewer, 9 tallest, 10 well.

6 0 - S E C O N D R E C A P

Adjective = noun, adverb = verb / adjective.

Linking verbs (look, feel, taste) + adjective.

Good = adjective, well = adverb.

Two things = -er / more + than; three or more = the -est / most.

Senior, junior, prefer + to.

Fewer = countable, less = uncountable.

OSASCOMP for adjective order.

gr-conjunctions.title: Conjunctions
gr-conjunctions.html:
Joining words  ·  + correlatives

A conjunction joins words, phrases or clauses. CUET tests which joining word fits the meaning, paired conjunctions and common wrong pairs.

PAGE 1
Types and MeaningCoordinating, subordinating and what each does

Start here: Which conjunction? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Decide the relationship (contrast, reason, result), then pick the word.

1.1 Coordinating conjunctions (FANBOYS)

FORreason He slept, for he was tired.
ANDaddition
Tea and coffee
NORnegative addition
Neither hot nor cold
BUTcontrast
Small but strong
ORchoice Tea or coffee?
YETsurprising contrast
Poor yet happy
SOresult It rained, so we left.
JOINequal parts two clauses of the same rank

1.2 Subordinating conjunctions by meaning

TIMEwhen, while, before, after, until, since Wait until I return.
REASONbecause, since, as Since you insist, I will go.
CONDITIONif, unless, provided that, as long as Unless you hurry, you will be late.
CONTRASTalthough, though, even though, whereas Although it rained, we played.
PURPOSEso that, in order that, lest Study so that you pass.
COMPARISONthan, as...as She is taller than I am.
M E M O R Y H A C K | F A N B O Y S

For And Nor But Or Yet So. These seven join equal parts, usually with a comma before them in a long sentence.

PAGE 2
Pairs and Special Rules
Correlatives and the tricky ones

2.1 Which pair? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

A pair is a team. Never mix the partners.

2.2 Rules that win marks

HARDLY / SCARCELY ... WHEN

not than

Hardly had he come when it rained.

NO SOONER ... THAN

not when

No sooner had he come than it rained.

UNLESSmeans "if not", so no extra not Unless you work, you will fail.
LESTfollowed by should, no not Walk fast lest you should be late.
THOUGH / ALTHOUGHdo not use but with them Although he was tired, he worked.
AS IF / AS THOUGHfollowed by past (unreal) He talks as if he were a king.
SINCE / FORsince = point, for = period since 2010, for ten years WHETHER ... OR NOT use whether for two choices I do not know whether he will come or not. BOTH ... AND not both...as well as Both he and she came.
E X A M T R A P S W I T H

Although and but never together: Although he is poor, but he is honest → Although he is poor, he is honest.

Unless already means "if not": Unless you do not work → Unless you work.

MEMORY HACK | HARDLY WHEN, NO SOONER THAN

Hardly / Scarcely pair with when. No sooner pairs with than. Both are followed by had + subject + V3.

PAGE 3

Traps, Practice and Recap

The mistakes examiners love, then test yourself

3.1 Pick the right pair at the end (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

The first half of a pair tells you the second half.

3.2 Favourite exam traps
WRONG
RIGHT
WHYAlthough he is poor, but he is honest Although he is poor, he is honest no but with although
Hardly had he come than it rained
Hardly had he come when it rainedhardly + when
No sooner had he come when it rained
No sooner had he come than it rainedno sooner + than Unless you do not work, you will fail Unless you work, you will fail unless already negative
Neither he or she came
Neither he nor she cameneither + nor
Either he nor she is wrong
Either he or she is wrongeither + or
Walk fast lest you will be late
Walk fast lest you should be latelest + should
I stayed because of it rained
I stayed because it rainedbecause + clause

3.3 Mixed practice: choose the right conjunction

1. (Although / Because) it was raining, we went out.

2. He is poor (but / because) honest.

3. Hardly had she left (than / when) the phone rang.

4. No sooner did he arrive (than / when) it began to rain.

5. (Unless / If) you hurry, you will miss the bus.

6. Neither Ram (or / nor) Shyam knew the answer.

7. Run fast (lest / so that) you miss the train.

8. He did not come (because / because of) he was ill.

9. You can have (either / neither) tea or coffee.

10. I do not know (whether / if) he will come or not.

Answers: 1 Although, 2 but, 3 when, 4 than, 5 Unless, 6 nor, 7 lest, 8 because, 9 either, 10 whether.

6 0 - S E C O N D R E C A P

FANBOYS join equal parts.

Although / though drop the but.

Hardly / scarcely ... when, no sooner ... than.

Unless = if not (no second negative).

Either ... or, neither ... nor, both ... and.

Lest ... should.

Because + clause, because of + noun.

gr-modals.title: Modals
gr-modals.html:
Can / May / Must  ·  + perfect modals

Modals (can, could, may, might, must, shall, should, will, would, need, dare, ought to) show ability, permission, duty, advice and possibility. A modal is always followed by the base verb (V1).

PAGE 1
What Each Modal MeansAbility, permission, duty and possibility

Start here: Which modal? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Name the idea first, then pick the modal.

1.1 Modals at a glance

CANability, informal permission She can speak French.
COULDpast ability, polite request Could you help me?
MAYpermission, possibility May I borrow your pen?
MIGHTweak possibility He might be late.
MUSTduty, strong certainty He must be at home.
SHOULDadvice, duty You should work harder.
WILLfuture, promise I will help you.
WOULDpast habit, polite He would visit us every summer.
SHALLI / we questions, offers Shall we begin?
M E M O R Y H A C K | M O D A L + V 1 , A L W A Y S

A modal is followed by the base verb, with no -s, -ed or -ing. She can sings → She can sing. He must goes → He must go.

PAGE 2
Rules and Perfect Modals
Past forms and the patterns CUET repeats

2.1 Modal for the past? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

For the past: modal + have + V3.

2.2 Rules that win marks

MUST VS HAVE TOmust = personal; have to = outside rule I must study. I have to wear a uniform. MUSTN'T VS NEEDN'T mustn't = forbidden; needn't = not necessary You mustn't smoke. You needn't come.
USED TOpast habit that stopped I used to play cricket.
NEED / DAREmodal in negatives and questions Need I go? He dare not speak.
OUGHT TOalways with to You ought to obey.
WOULD RATHERpreference, then V1 I would rather stay.
HAD BETTERstrong advice, then V1 You had better leave now.
CAN / MAYcan = ability; may = permission May I go out?
NO DOUBLE MODALSonly one modal in a clause She will can come → She will be able to come.
E X A M T R A P S W I T H

Two modals together are wrong: You should must go.

Ought needs to: You ought obey → You ought to obey.

Mustn't and needn't are not the same.

M E M O R Y H A C K | S H O U L D H A V E = R E G R E T

should have + V3 = a past mistake. must have + V3 = a past guess you are sure about. You should have studied. / He must have forgotten.

PAGE 3

Traps, Practice and Recap

The mistakes examiners love, then test yourself

3.1 Must, have to, mustn't or needn't? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Mustn't = never; needn't = no need.

3.2 Favourite exam traps
WRONG
RIGHT
WHY
She can sings well
She can sing wellmodal + V1
You ought obey rules
You ought to obey rulesought to
You should must go
You must goone modal only He can not enter (rule)
He must not enterforbidden = mustn't
You should told me yesterday
You should have told me yesterdaypast advice = should have + V3
You need not to go
You need not goneed not + V1
I used to going
I used to goused to + V1
I wish I can fly
I wish I could flypast form after wish

3.3 Mixed practice: choose the right modal

1. (May / Can) I use your phone? (polite request)

2. He (must / might) be at home; the lights are on.

3. You (should have / will have) listened to me.

4. You (mustn't / needn't) hurry; there is plenty of time.

5. She can (swim / swims) very well.

6. You (ought / ought to) respect elders.

7. You (had better / had) leave now.

8. I (would rather / will rather) stay home.

9. He (used to / use to) play football.

10. (Could / Must) you pass the salt, please?

Answers: 1 May, 2 must, 3 should have, 4 needn't, 5 swim, 6 ought to, 7 had better, 8 would rather, 9 used to, 10 Could.

6 0 - S E C O N D R E C A P

Modal + V1 always.

Can = ability; may = permission; must = duty; should = advice.

Mustn't = forbidden; needn't = not necessary.

Past: should have / must have / may have + V3.

Ought to, used to, would rather, had better + V1.

One modal per clause.

gr-voice.title: Active & Passive Voice
gr-voice.html:
Doer / Receiver  ·  + all tenses

In active voice the subject does the action; in passive voice the subject receives it. The passive is built as be + V3. CUET asks you to convert or to choose the correct passive.

PAGE 1
Making the PassiveThe recipe and the be-form for every tense

Start here: Convert to passive (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Only verbs with an object (transitive) can become passive.

1.1 The passive for each tense

PRESENT SIMPLEis / am / are + V3 Letters are written daily.
PRESENT CONTINUOUSis / am / are being + V3 A letter is being written.
PRESENT PERFECThas / have been + V3 A letter has been written.
PAST SIMPLEwas / were + V3 A letter was written.
PAST CONTINUOUSwas / were being + V3 A letter was being written.
PAST PERFECThad been + V3 A letter had been written.
FUTURE SIMPLEwill be + V3 A letter will be written.
MODALSmodal + be + V3 A letter can be written.
FUTURE PERFECTwill have been + V3 A letter will have been written.
M E M O R Y H A C K | 3 S T E P S

1. Object becomes subject. 2. Verb becomes be + V3 (be in the same tense). 3. Subject becomes by + object (or drops). Ram ate a mango → A mango was eaten by Ram.

PAGE 2
Special PassivesQuestions, commands and tricky verbs

2.1 Which type of sentence? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

The sentence type decides how you start the passive.

2.2 Rules that win marks

IMPERATIVE
Let + object + be + V3Close the window. → Let the window be closed.
REQUESTYou are requested to ... Please sit. → You are requested to sit.
INTERROGATIVE
Do / does / did disappearsDid she write it? → Was it written by her?
WH- QUESTIONS
Wh- word stays firstWho wrote it? → By whom was it written?
VERBS WITH 2 OBJECTSeither object can be the subject He gave me a book. → I was given a book.
INTRANSITIVE VERBSno passive He was slept.
STATIVE VERBShave, resemble, lack: no passive A car is had by him.
INFINITIVEto be + V3 He wants to be told.
GERUNDbeing + V3 I like being praised.
E X A M T R A P S W I T H

Never drop "be": The letter written by her → The letter was written by her.

V3 after be: The cake was eat → was eaten.

Wh- questions: "Who" becomes "by whom".

M E M O R Y H A C K | P A S S I V E = B E + V 3

No matter the tense, passive = be-form + V3. Only the be-form changes: is, was, will be, has been, had been, is being, was being.

PAGE 3

Traps, Practice and Recap

The mistakes examiners love, then test yourself

3.1 Active or passive? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Doer = active. Receiver = passive.

3.2 Favourite exam traps
WRONG
RIGHT
WHY
The cake was ate by him
The cake was eaten by himbe + V3
The letter written by her
The letter was written by herbe is needed
The work has done
The work has been donehas been + V3
The room is cleaning now
The room is being cleaned nowis being + V3 By whom it was written? By whom was it written? question order
He was slept well
He slept wellintransitive
A car is had by him
He has a carhave stays active
Let the door opened
Let the door be openedlet + be + V3

3.3 Mixed practice: convert to passive

1. She sings a song. → A song ___ by her.

2. They are building a bridge. → A bridge ___ built.

3. He has finished the work. → The work ___ finished.

4. Ram will help me. → I ___ helped by Ram.

5. Who broke the glass? → By whom ___ the glass broken?

6. Open the door. → Let the door ___ opened.

7. The cook was preparing dinner. → Dinner ___ prepared.

8. Did she win the prize? → ___ the prize won by her?

9. They gave him a prize. → He ___ given a prize.

10. We must obey rules. → Rules must ___ obeyed.

Answers: 1 is sung, 2 is being, 3 has been, 4 will be, 5 was, 6 be, 7 was being, 8 Was, 9 was, 10 be.

6 0 - S E C O N D R E C A P

Passive = be + V3 in the same tense as the active verb.

Object becomes subject, subject becomes by + object.

Continuous: is / was being + V3.

Perfect: has / have / had been + V3.

Command: let + be + V3.

No passive for intransitive or stative verbs.

gr-speech.title: Direct & Indirect Speech
gr-speech.html:
Reporting words  ·  + tense back-shift

Direct speech gives the exact words in quotes. Indirect speech reports them without quotes, usually with a tense shift, pronoun change and time or place change.

PAGE 1
Making Indirect SpeechTense, pronoun and word changes

Start here: Convert to indirect (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

The reporting verb decides if the tense moves.

1.1 Tense back-shift

PRESENT SIMPLE→ past simple "I eat" → he said he ate.
PRESENT CONTINUOUS→ past continuous "I am eating" → he said he was eating.
PRESENT PERFECT→ past perfect "I have eaten" → he said he had eaten.
PAST SIMPLE→ past perfect "I ate" → he said he had eaten.
WILL / CAN / MAY→ would / could / might "I will go" → he said he would go.
PAST PERFECTno change "I had eaten" → he said he had eaten.

1.2 Word changes

NOW→ then
TODAY→ that day
TOMORROW→ the next day
YESTERDAY→ the day before
HERE→ there
THIS→ that
AGO→ before
LAST NIGHT→ the night before
M E M O R Y H A C K | P N T

Change three things: Pronoun, Now-words (time and place), Tense. He said, "I am here now." → He said that he was there then.

PAGE 2

Questions, Commands and Exclamations

Each sentence type has its own link word

2.1 Which reporting verb? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Question = if / whether. Command = to. Statement = that.

2.2 Rules that win marks

WH- QUESTIONSkeep the wh- word, drop the question order "Where do you live?" → He asked me where I lived.
COMMANDStold / ordered + to "Sit down." → He told me to sit down.
REQUESTSrequested / begged + to "Please help." → He requested me to help.
ADVICEadvised + to "You should rest." → He advised me to rest.
NEGATIVE COMMANDtold + not to "Do not run." → He told me not to run. LET'S suggested + -ing "Let's go." → He suggested going.
WISHESwished + noun "Good luck!" → He wished me good luck.
GREETINGSwished / greeted "Good morning" → He wished me good morning.
THANKSthanked "Thank you" → He thanked me.
E X A M T R A P S W I T H

No question mark and no inverted order in indirect speech: He asked where did I live → He asked where I lived.

Say has no object; tell needs one: He told that → He told me that / He said that.

M E M O R Y H A C K | S A Y T O T E L L , A S K T O A S K

"Say to" becomes told (statement) or asked (question). He said to me, "Go." → He told me to go.

PAGE 3

Traps, Practice and Recap

The mistakes examiners love, then test yourself

3.1 Which connector? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Wh- stays, yes/no gets if.

3.2 Favourite exam traps
WRONG
RIGHT
WHY
He asked where did I live
He asked where I livedno inversion
He told that he was ill
He said that he was illtold needs an object
He said me that he was ill
He told me that he was illtold + object
She asked that I was ill
She asked if I was illyes/no = if He said that he is ill (past report)
He said that he was illback-shift
He said that he will go tomorrow
He said that he would go the next daytime word change
He told me do it
He told me to do itcommand = to + V1
He said me to go
He told me to gosaid → told

3.3 Mixed practice: convert to indirect speech

1. He said, "I am ill." → He said that he ___ ill.

2. She said, "I have finished." → She said that she ___ finished.

3. He asked, "Where do you live?" → He asked me where I ___.

4. He said to me, "Go home." → He ___ me to go home.

5. She said, "I will come tomorrow." → She said that she would come ___.

6. He asked, "Are you tired?" → He asked me ___ I was tired.

7. The teacher said, "The earth moves." → The teacher said that the earth ___.

8. He said, "Do not talk." → He told me ___ to talk.

9. She said, "I saw him yesterday." → She said she ___ him the day before.

10. He said, "Let us go." → He ___ going.

Answers: 1 was, 2 had, 3 lived, 4 told, 5 the next day, 6 if / whether, 7 moves, 8 not, 9 had seen, 10 suggested.

6 0 - S E C O N D R E C A P

PNT: change Pronoun, Now-words, Tense.

Past reporting verb → back-shift; universal truth stays.

Wh- question: keep the wh- word, no inversion.

Yes / no: if / whether.

Command: told + to.

Say has no object, tell has one.

gr-error-detection.title: Error Detection / Spotting Errors
gr-error-detection.html:
Spot the Mistake  ·  + 10 usual suspects

In error detection you read four parts of a sentence and find the part with the mistake. Scan for the usual suspects in a fixed order and you will be fast and accurate.

PAGE 1
The Scan Order
Check the same things in the same order

Start here: The error-spotting checklist (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

If you scan in this order, the mistake rarely escapes.

1.1 The ten usual suspects

1 SUBJECT-VERB

verb must match the subject

The list of items are long → is

2 TENSE

time word vs tense

I have seen him yesterday → saw

3 ARTICLES

a / an / the

She is a honest girl → an

4 PREPOSITIONS

fixed pairs

He is good in maths → at

5 PRONOUNS

case and agreement

Between you and I → me

6 ADJECTIVES / ADVERBS

which word?

She sings good → well

7 CONJUNCTIONS

pairs

Hardly...than → when

8 MODALS

modal + V1

He can goes → go

9 DEGREES

no double comparison

more better → better

M E M O R Y H A C K | S - T - A - P - P - A - C

Subject-verb, Tense, Article, Preposition, Pronoun, Adjective/adverb, Conjunction. Check them in this order.

PAGE 2
Spot It Fast
Signals and patterns

2.1 If you see X, check Y (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

A signal word tells you which rule is being tested.

2.2 Signal → Check

TWO THINGS COMPAREDcheck comparative She is taller than me (not more taller)
THE + ADJECTIVEplural meaning The poor are (not is)
EACH / EVERYsingular verb and pronoun
Each boy has his pen
UNCOUNTABLEfurniture, advice, news: no plural
The furniture is new
IF / WHEN CLAUSEpresent, not will If it rains, we stay
PAST HABITused to + V1
He used to play cricket
PREFERto not than
I prefer tea to coffeeLOOK, FEEL, TASTE adjective follows She looks happy, not happily
NO ERRORif all checks pass, choose No error
E X A M T R A P S W I T H

Do not hunt only for big mistakes. Many errors are tiny: a / an, s / es, to / for.

Read the full sentence once before you underline a part.

If you are 50% sure of an error, go with it; "No error" is only the answer about once in five.

M E M O R Y H A C K | R E A D A G A I N , S L O W E R

Read once for meaning, once for grammar. If every part looks fine, run the S-T-A-P-P-A-C checklist one letter at a time.

PAGE 3

Traps, Practice and Recap

Test yourself on mixed errors

3.1 If no error stands out (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Choose "No error" last, not first.

3.2 Favourite exam traps
WRONG
RIGHT
WHY
The list of items are long
The list of items is longhead noun is list
I have seen him yesterday
I saw him yesterdayfinished time
She is a honest girl
She is an honest girlsilent h
He is good in maths
He is good at mathsgood at
Between you and I
Between you and mebetween + object
She sings good
She sings welladverb
Hardly had he come than
Hardly had he come whenhardly + when
He is more smarter
He is smarterno double comparison

3.3 Mixed practice: which part has the error?

1. Each of the players / have / been given / a medal. (a, b, c, d)

2. He did not / came / to school / yesterday.

3. She is / one of the / best player / in the team.

4. I have been / living here / since / five years.

5. The news / were / shocking / to all.

6. If it / will rain / we shall / stay home.

7. He has / a few / knowledge / of Hindi.

8. Neither Ram / nor Shyam / are / coming.

9. She prefers / coffee / than / tea.

10. Mathematics / is / a / interesting subject.

Answers: 1 b (has), 2 b (come), 3 c (best players), 4 c (for), 5 b (was), 6 b (rains), 7 b (little), 8 c (is), 9 c (to), 10 c (an).

6 0 - S E C O N D R E C A P

Check in order: S-V, tense, article, preposition, pronoun, adjective / adverb, conjunction.

Signal words point to the rule: since, each, hardly, unless.

Small words (a / an, to / for) hide most errors.

No error only when every check passes.

Read twice: once for sense, once for grammar.

gr-sentence-correction.title: Sentence Correction
gr-sentence-correction.html:
Best Replacement  ·  + 4-step method

In sentence correction an underlined part may be wrong. You choose the best replacement from the options, or pick "no improvement". The trick is find the error type first, then eliminate options.

PAGE 1
The 4-Step Method
How to attack every question

Start here: Attack plan (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Read the whole sentence, find the error type, then test each option.

1.1 The four steps

STEP 1 READRead the full sentence once for meaning, not just the underlined part.
STEP 2 SPOTRun the checklist: S-V, tense, pronoun, parallel structure, modifier.
STEP 3 ELIMINATECross out options that repeat the error or add a new one.
STEP 4 RE-READPut your choice into the sentence and read it again aloud in your head.

1.2 What is usually tested

AGREEMENTsubject and verb The boys play (not plays)
TENSEtime words
He left yesterday
PARALLEL STRUCTUREsame form in a list She likes singing, dancing and painting
PRONOUNcase and reference
She and I went
MODIFIERplace next to the noun Walking home, I met a friend
REDUNDANCYno repeated meaning return (not return back)
M E M O R Y H A C K | O P T I O N A = S A M E

Option A usually repeats the original. Choose it only when you have checked all the error types and found none.

PAGE 2
Common Fixes
Patterns that appear again and again

2.1 What kind of fix? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Four fix types cover most sentence-correction questions.

2.2 Rules that win marks

PARALLELISMlist items in the same form He likes to read, to write and to draw.
DANGLING MODIFIERthe -ing doer must be the subject Walking home, a dog bit me → Walking home, I was bitten by a dog.
REDUNDANCYavoid double meaning return back, repeat again, free gift
WORDINESSprefer the short phrase due to the fact that → because
COMPARISONcompare like with like The climate of Delhi is hotter than that of Shimla.
DOUBLE NEGATIVEone negative only I do not know nothing → I know nothing.
SUBJUNCTIVEif I were If I were you, I would go.
PRONOUN REFERENCEbe clear who "it" is When Ram met Mohan, he smiled (who?)
TENSE SEQUENCEkeep the same time He said he would come.
E X A M T R A P S W I T H

Dangling modifiers: the noun after the comma must be the one doing the -ing action.

Wrong comparison: Delhi's climate is hotter than Shimla → than that of Shimla.

Redundancy is usually wrong in an option; shorter is safer.

M E M O R Y H A C K | S H O R T A N D C L E A R W I N S

When two options are both grammatical, choose the shorter, clearer one. Examiners reward clean sentences.

PAGE 3

Traps, Practice and Recap

The mistakes examiners love, then test yourself

3.1 Which option? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Eliminate first, choose last.

3.2 Favourite exam traps
WRONG
RIGHT
WHYWalking home, a dog bit me Walking home, I was bitten by a dog dangling modifier She likes to swim, running and dancing She likes swimming, running and dancing parallel
Please return back the book
Please return the bookredundant
Delhi is hotter than Shimla
Delhi is hotter than that of Shimlacompare like with like
I do not know nothing
I know nothing / I do not know anythingdouble negative If I was you, I would go If I were you, I would go unreal condition
The reason is because he was ill
The reason is that he was illreason + that
The books of Ram are better than ShyamThe books of Ram are better than Shyam's compare like with like

3.3 Mixed practice: choose the best replacement

1. The boys ___ (is / are) playing outside.

2. She likes reading, writing and ___ (to paint / painting).

3. If I ___ (was / were) rich, I would help them.

4. Please ___ (return back / return) the book.

5. The weather of Delhi is hotter than ___ (Shimla / that of Shimla).

6. ___ (Running to the station / When he ran to the station), the bag fell.

7. The reason he left is ___ (because / that) he was angry.

8. He ___ (did not come / did not came) yesterday.

9. Each of the students ___ (has / have) a book.

10. Hardly had she left ___ (when / than) it rained.

Answers: 1 are, 2 painting, 3 were, 4 return, 5 that of Shimla, 6 When he ran to the station, 7 that, 8 did not come, 9 has, 10 when.

6 0 - S E C O N D R E C A P

Four steps: read, spot, eliminate, re-read.

Parallel lists use the same form.

Dangling modifier: doer must follow the comma.

Compare like with like (that of).

Redundancy is wrong (return back).

Option A is correct only if no error is found.

gr-conditionals.title: Conditionals
gr-conditionals.html:
If Sentences  ·  + types 0 to 3

A conditional sentence has an if-clause (condition) and a main clause (result). There are four types, and the tense of the if-clause tells you the type.

PAGE 1
The Four TypesZero, first, second and third conditional

Start here: Which conditional? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Look at the if-clause verb. It names the type.

1.1 The four types

ZERO (ALWAYS TRUE)

If + present, present

If you heat water, it boils.

FIRST (REAL, LIKELY)

If + present, will + V1

If you study, you will pass.

SECOND (UNREAL, PRESENT)

If + past, would + V1

If I knew, I would tell you.

THIRD (UNREAL, PAST)

If + had + V3, would have + V3

If I had known, I would have told you.

M E M O R Y H A C K | 1 - 2 - 3

1st: present → will. 2nd: past → would. 3rd: had V3 → would have V3. The if-clause tense goes one step back each time.

PAGE 2
Rules and VariationsUnless, were, mixed types and inversion

2.1 Special if-patterns (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

These three patterns appear in many exam sentences.

2.2 Rules that win marks

NO WILL AFTER IFif-clause never takes will / would If it rains, not if it will rain
UNLESSalready negative, so no not Unless you work, you will fail
IF I WEREwere for all persons in unreal if-clauses If he were here, he would help.
MIXED TYPEpast condition, present result If I had studied, I would be a doctor now.
INVERSIONdrop if, move had / were / should Had she known, she would have come.
PROVIDED / AS LONG ASmean "only if" You may go provided you return early.
IN CASEprecaution Take an umbrella in case it rains.
WISHunreal present = past, unreal past = had V3 I wish I had time. I wish I had known.
OTHERWISE / ORimply an if Hurry up, or you will be late.
E X A M T R A P S W I T H

Never use will in the if-clause: If you will come, I will go → If you come, I will go.

Never use would in the if-clause: If I would know → If I knew.

Unless + negative is wrong.

MEMORY HACK | WOULD STAYS IN THE RESULT

would / would have belong only in the result clause. The if-clause takes the tense, never would.

Traps, Practice and Recap

The mistakes examiners love, then test yourself

decision flowchart

3.2 Favourite exam traps
WRONG
RIGHT
WHYIf it will rain, we will stay If it rains, we will stay no will in the if-clause If I would know, I would tell If I knew, I would tell no would in if-clause If I was you, I would go If I were you, I would go were for unreal
Unless you do not work
Unless you workunless = if not If I knew, I would have told you If I had known, I would have told you third conditional If you study, you would pass If you study, you will pass first conditional If I have time, I would help If I had time, I would help second conditional Had I known, I will help you Had I known, I would have helped you third conditional result

3.3 Mixed practice: complete the sentence

1. If it rains, we ___ (will stay / would stay) home.

2. If I ___ (was / were) you, I would apologise.

3. If she had studied, she ___ (would pass / would have passed).

4. Unless you ___ (hurry / do not hurry), you will be late.

5. If you heat ice, it ___ (melts / will melt).

6. ___ (Had / Have) I known, I would have helped.

7. I wish I ___ (have / had) more time.

8. If I ___ (had / have) a car, I would drive you.

9. He will help you provided you ___ (ask / will ask).

10. If I had left earlier, I ___ (would be / will be) there now.

Answers: 1 will stay, 2 were, 3 would have passed, 4 hurry, 5 melts, 6 Had, 7 had, 8 had, 9 ask, 10 would be.

6 0 - S E C O N D R E C A P

Type 1: if + present, will + V1.

Type 2: if + past, would + V1.

Type 3: if + had V3, would have V3.

Zero: if + present, present (facts).

Unless = if not.

If I were for all persons.

No will / would in the if-clause.

gr-question-tags.title: Question Tags
gr-question-tags.html:
Isn't it?  ·  + opposite rule

A question tag is a short question added to a statement ("...isn't it?"). The rule is simple: positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag, using the same helping verb and a pronoun.

PAGE 1
The Opposite Rule
Build a tag in three steps

Start here: Build the tag (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Opposite sign, same helping verb, pronoun at the end.

1.1 Three steps

STEP 1 FLIP THE SIGNpositive → negative; negative → positive He is here, isn't he?
STEP 2 SAME VERBrepeat the helping verb She has gone, hasn't she?
STEP 3 USE A PRONOUNnever a noun Ram is kind, isn't he?

1.2 Examples by tense

PRESENT SIMPLEdo / does You like tea, don't you?
PAST SIMPLEdid He left, didn't he?
FUTUREwill She will come, won't she?
PERFECThas / have / had They have gone, haven't they?
MODALSsame modal You can swim, can't you?
CONTINUOUSis / are / was He is reading, isn't he?
M E M O R Y H A C K | F L I P , C O P Y , S W A P

Flip the sign, copy the helping verb, swap the noun for a pronoun. Ram can swim, can't he?

PAGE 2
Special Cases
The exceptions CUET loves

2.1 Special statements (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Memorise these three special tags.

2.2 Rules that win marks

I AM ...

aren't I

I am right, aren't I?

LET US / LET'S

shall we

Let us go, shall we?

COMMANDSwill you Close the door, will you?
NEGATIVE COMMANDwill you Don't go, will you? NOBODY, NO ONE, NONE positive tag with they Nobody came, did they? EVERYONE, SOMEONE tag with they Everyone knows, don't they? SELDOM, HARDLY, NEVER count as negative → positive tag He never lies, does he?
THERE IS / THERE AREtag keeps there There is a pen, isn't there?
THIS / THATtag with it This is easy, isn't it?
E X A M T R A P S W I T H

Never use a noun in the tag: Ram is kind, isn't Ram → isn't he.

Hardly / seldom / never make the statement negative: He hardly speaks, doesn't he → does he.

I am takes aren't I, not amn't I.

M E M O R Y H A C K | N E G A T I V E W O R D S F L I P T O O

Words like never, seldom, rarely, hardly, nobody, nothing are negative. The tag is therefore positive: She seldom comes, does she?

PAGE 3

Traps, Practice and Recap

The mistakes examiners love, then test yourself

3.1 Choose the tag quickly (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Check for hidden negatives before you build the tag.

3.2 Favourite exam traps
WRONG
RIGHT
WHYI am late, amn't I? I am late, aren't I? special tag Let's go, don't we? Let's go, shall we? let's He hardly speaks, doesn't he? He hardly speaks, does he? hardly is negative Nobody came, didn't they? Nobody came, did they? nobody is negative Open the door, won't you? Open the door, will you? command Ram is kind, isn't Ram? Ram is kind, isn't he? pronoun She sings well, isn't she? She sings well, doesn't she? do / does There is a pen, isn't it? There is a pen, isn't there? there stays

3.3 Mixed practice: add the tag

1. She is a doctor, ___?

2. They have finished, ___?

3. You do not like tea, ___?

4. Let us start, ___?

5. Close the window, ___?

6. He never cheats, ___?

7. I am correct, ___?

8. Everyone enjoyed the film, ___?

9. There are five boys, ___?

10. He can swim, ___?

Answers: 1 isn't she, 2 haven't they, 3 do you, 4 shall we, 5 will you, 6 does he, 7 aren't I, 8 didn't they, 9 aren't there, 10 can't he.

6 0 - S E C O N D R E C A P

Opposite sign: positive → negative, negative → positive.

Same helping verb; no helper → do / does / did.

I am → aren't I.

Let's → shall we.

Command → will you.

Never, hardly, nobody → positive tag.

Pronoun in the tag, never a noun.

gr-parts-of-speech.title: Parts of Speech
gr-parts-of-speech.html:
8 Parts  ·  + job test

Every word has a job. A word's part of speech depends on how it is used, not on its spelling. CUET asks you to identify the part of speech of an underlined word.

PAGE 1
The Eight Parts
What each part does

Start here: What is this word? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Ask: what job is this word doing in this sentence?

1.1 The eight parts

NOUNnames Delhi, courage
PRONOUNreplaces a noun She, they
VERBaction / state run, is
ADJECTIVEdescribes a noun tall boy
ADVERBdescribes verb / adj runs fast
PREPOSITIONlinks noun on the table
CONJUNCTIONjoins tea and coffee
INTERJECTIONemotion Alas! Wow!

1.2 Types worth knowing

NOUN TYPEScommon, proper, collective, abstract, material India, team, honesty
VERB TYPESmain, auxiliary, modal She has gone. He can sing.
ADVERB TYPESmanner, time, place, degree slowly, today, here, very
M E M O R Y H A C K | P A V A P C N I

Pronoun, Adverb, Verb, Adjective, Preposition, Conjunction, Noun, Interjection. Eight jobs, eight parts.

PAGE 2
The Job TestSame word, different part of speech

2.1 One word, many jobs (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Position in the sentence shows the part of speech.

2.2 Rules that win marks

NOUN TESTcan follow the / a the book, a hope
VERB TESTchanges with tense walk / walked / will walk
ADJECTIVE TESTcan follow very or be very tall, She is kind.
ADVERB TESToften ends -ly, answers how / when / where quickly, soon, there
PREPOSITION TESTcomes before a noun in the room, at noon
CONJUNCTION TESTjoins two parts He came but left. SAME WORD, TWO JOBS after: preposition or conjunction After lunch (prep). After he left (conj).
FASTadjective or adverb a fast train (adj); runs fast (adv)
ROUNDnoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition a round table (adj)
E X A M T R A P S W I T H

Do not judge by spelling: "early" is an adverb — it can also be an adjective (the early bird).

Words ending in -ly are not always adverbs: friendly, lovely, lonely are adjectives.

M E M O R Y H A C K | A S K 3 Q U E S T I O N S

What does it do? What comes before it? What comes after it? Noun after the, verb after the subject, adjective before the noun, adverb near the verb.

PAGE 3

Traps, Practice and Recap

The mistakes examiners love, then test yourself

3.1 Quick identification (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Joining word? Linking word? Describing word?

3.2 Favourite exam traps
WRONG
RIGHT
WHY"lovely" is an adverb "lovely" is an adjective ends -ly but describes "fast" in "runs fast" is an adjective "fast" is an adverb describes the verb "after" is always a conjunction "after" can be a preposition too depends on use "hard" in "works hard" is a noun "hard" is an adverb describes the verb "light" in "a light bag" is a noun "light" is an adjective before the noun "Alas" is a noun "Alas" is an interjection shows emotion "but" is an adverb "but" is a conjunction joins "well" in "sings well" is an adjective "well" is an adverb describes the verb

3.3 Mixed practice: name the part of speech

1. The lion roared. (noun / verb)

2. She quickly left. (adjective / adverb)

3. It is a beautiful day. (adjective / noun)

4. He is in the room. (preposition / adverb)

5. Tea and coffee are hot. (conjunction / pronoun)

6. Wow! That is amazing. (interjection / noun)

7. She is kind. (adjective / verb)

8. He runs fast. (noun / verb)

9. They won. (pronoun / noun)

10. He works hard. (adjective / adverb)

Answers: 1 noun, 2 adverb, 3 adjective, 4 preposition, 5 conjunction, 6 interjection, 7 adjective, 8 verb, 9 pronoun, 10 adverb.

6 0 - S E C O N D R E C A P

Eight parts: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction, interjection.

Job decides the part, not spelling.

Adjective before a noun; adverb near the verb.

-ly does not always mean adverb (lovely, friendly).

After / before can be preposition or conjunction.

gr-literary-devices.title: Literary Devices
gr-literary-devices.html:
Figures of Speech  ·  + 12 devices

Literary devices are tools writers use to make language vivid. CUET asks you to name the device in a line. Learn the clue words and you can identify almost any device.

PAGE 1
Comparison DevicesSimile, metaphor, personification and more

Start here: Which device? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Look for like / as first, then for "is", then for human actions.

1.1 Comparison devices

SIMILEcompare with like / as as cold as ice, like a rose
METAPHORdirect comparison Life is a journey.
PERSONIFICATIONhuman traits for non-human The sun smiled on us.
HYPERBOLEextreme exaggeration I have told you a million times.
ONOMATOPOEIAsound words buzz, hiss, bang, splash
APOSTROPHEtalking to an absent thing O Death, where is thy sting?
M E M O R Y H A C K | L I K E A S = S I M I L E

See like or as between two things? Simile. No like / as, just "is"? Metaphor. A thing doing human actions? Personification.

PAGE 2
Sound and Meaning DevicesAlliteration, irony, oxymoron and more

2.1 Which sound or meaning device? (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Sound repeated = alliteration. Opposite words = oxymoron. Opposite meaning = irony.

2.2 More devices

ALLITERATIONsame starting sound Sally sells seashells.
ASSONANCEsame vowel sound The rain in Spain.
OXYMORONtwo opposites together Living death, cruel kindness
IRONYopposite of what is expected A pilot afraid of heights.
PARADOXseems false but true Less is more.
EUPHEMISMsoft word for harsh one passed away (died)
PUNplay on a word "I used to be a banker, but I lost interest."
ANTITHESIScontrasting ideas in balance To err is human, to forgive divine.
ANAPHORAsame word starts lines We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight in the fields.
E X A M T R A P S W I T H

Simile vs metaphor: like / as = simile. "He is as brave as a lion" is a metaphor.

Oxymoron vs paradox: oxymoron is two words (deafening silence); paradox is a whole statement.

Irony vs sarcasm: sarcasm is spoken and sharp; irony is a situation or words.

M E M O R Y H A C K | O X Y - M O R O N = S M A R T F O O L

Oxymoron = a "sharp" and "foolish" word together. Opposite words side by side: a wise fool, bitter sweet, open secret.

PAGE 3

Traps, Practice and Recap

The mistakes examiners love, then test yourself

3.1 Name the device (follow the arrows)

decision flowchart

Quick checks name most devices.

3.2 Favourite exam traps
WRONG
RIGHT
WHY"as brave as a lion" is a metaphor "as brave as a lion" is a simile as...as "Time is a thief" is a simile "Time is a thief" is a metaphor no like / as "The wind whispered" is a metaphor "The wind whispered" is personification human action "deafening silence" is irony "deafening silence" is an oxymoron two opposite words "I am so hungry I could eat a horse" is a metaphor
It is hyperboleexaggeration "buzz, hiss" show alliteration
They show onomatopoeiasound words "Less is more" is an oxymoron "Less is more" is a paradox whole statement "passed away" is a metaphor "passed away" is a euphemism soft word for died

3.3 Mixed practice: name the device

1. The wind howled angrily.

2. He is as strong as an ox.

3. The classroom was a zoo.

4. Peter picked a pickled pepper.

5. A pilot afraid of flying.

6. I have a million things to do.

7. The thunder boomed.

8. It was a bittersweet farewell.

9. Less is more.

10. He passed away peacefully.

Answers: 1 personification, 2 simile, 3 metaphor, 4 alliteration, 5 irony, 6 hyperbole, 7 onomatopoeia, 8 oxymoron, 9 paradox, 10 euphemism.

6 0 - S E C O N D R E C A P

Simile = like / as; metaphor = is.

Personification = human actions for things.

Hyperbole = exaggeration.

Alliteration = same starting sound.

Oxymoron = two opposite words.

Irony = opposite of expected.

Paradox = seems false, is true.

Euphemism = soft word.
